primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Classic Menkes disease due to ATP7A dysfunction
mechanism: ATP7A encodes a P-type copper-transporting ATPase that transports copper across cellular membranes and is essential for intestinal copper absorption and tissue copper distribution. Severe ATP7A loss of function produces systemic copper deficiency and reduced activity of multiple copper-dependent enzymes.
vignette: A 3-month-old boy who appeared healthy at birth develops failure to thrive, hypotonia, and seizures. His scalp hair is sparse, coarse, twisted, and lightly pigmented. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin concentrations are low. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic loss-of-function variant in ATP7A.
lead: Which of the following cellular defects most directly causes this disorder?
correct: Impaired ATP-dependent copper transport across cellular membranes, reducing intestinal copper absorption and tissue distribution
distractors: Impaired ATP-dependent biliary copper excretion from hepatocytes
Defective intestinal iron export through ferroportin
Failure to incorporate iron into protoporphyrin IX in erythroid precursors
Reduced endosomal release of vitamin B12 from transcobalamin
distractor_notes: Impaired ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion causes Wilson disease with copper accumulation, not Menkes disease with systemic copper deficiency.
Ferroportin mediates cellular iron export; defects cause iron-loading or iron-restricted phenotypes rather than ATP7A-related copper deficiency.
Failure to insert iron into protoporphyrin IX involves heme synthesis and does not explain kinky hair, low copper, and ATP7A mutation.
Vitamin B12 trafficking defects do not cause the copper-deficiency phenotype or characteristic hair abnormalities of Menkes disease.
key_expl: ATP7A is a P-type ATPase that transports copper across cellular membranes. Severe ATP7A dysfunction impairs intestinal copper absorption and normal tissue distribution, causing low systemic copper availability and reduced function of copper-dependent enzymes. Classic Menkes disease presents in early infancy with neurodegeneration, seizures, failure to thrive, and characteristic sparse kinky hair.
objective: Identify Menkes disease as an ATP7A-mediated copper-transport defect causing impaired copper absorption/distribution and systemic copper-enzyme deficiency.
